t: Find Nearest Point That Has the Same X or Y Coordinate in One Pass
o: A point is valid when it shares our x or our y coordinate; among valid points we want the smallest Manhattan distance, resolving ties by smallest index. For aligned points the Manhattan formula degenerates nicely: it is |a-x| when b equals y, |b-y| when a equals x. Example 1: valid points [3,1],[2,4],[4,4] have distances 3,1,1, and the index-2 point wins the tie. Example 2 allows the point sitting exactly on our location (distance 0). Example 3 has no valid point, giving -1. With n up to 10^4, a single scan with O(1) state is trivially optimal.
k: Validity check is a simple OR: a == x or b == y; the Manhattan distance then needs no squares or sqrt.
Updating the best only on STRICT improvement while scanning left to right makes the smallest index win ties for free.
One comparison per point is unbeatable: O(n) time, O(1) space.

a.n: Approach 1: Single Pass Tracking the Best
a.i: Sweep points left to right carrying (bestDistance, bestIndex). Skip invalid points; for valid ones compute the distance and replace the incumbent only when strictly smaller. Order plus strictness guarantees the earliest index prevails among equal distances.
s: For each i, if a == x or b == y compute d = |a-x| + |b-y|.
If d < best, update best = d and ans = i.

a.n: Approach 2: Collect Candidates, Sort, Take First
a.i: Gather (distance, index) pairs for all valid points, sort them lexicographically, and read the first pair index. More work than necessary here, but the pattern generalizes to richer criteria such as secondary tiebreakers beyond index.
s: Collect (d, i) for every valid point.
If the collection is empty return -1.
Sort pairs by distance, then index.
Return the index of the first pair.
a.t: O(n log n) - dominated by sorting up to n candidates

w: Always present approach 1 first; it is both simplest and optimal. Pitfalls: forgetting the -1 case when nothing validates, using <= in the update (which breaks the smallest-index tie-break), and needlessly squaring coordinates. Follow-ups: k nearest valid points (size-k heap), or validity extended to rows/columns within a rectangle - the scan pattern stays identical while the filter changes.
